newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish socialists propose successor to Gonzalez.
newsitem.headline: Spanish socialists propose successor to Gonzalez.

text.p: Spain's Socialist leaders recommended on Saturday that party members elect veteran politician Joaquin Almunia to replace his longtime ally, former Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez, as party chief.

Meeting behind closed doors, the executive committee decided that Almunia, who worked for years in Gonzalez' shadow but had rarely been mentioned as a possible successor, was the best candidate to assume the top leadership role, officials said.

The announcement came one day after Gonzalez, who led Spain for 13 years until his electoral defeat in 1996, stunned his supporters by telling them he would not run again as Socialist secretary-general.
That gave party leaders only 48 hours to come up with a replacement.
Almunia, 49, a former government minister and labor union boss, emerged as the top choice from a list of Socialist heavyweights that included regional presidents, national deputies and city mayors.
The 1,000-member party congress was expected to vote on the leadership's recommendation on Sunday.
"I would say it was unanimous that Joaquin Almunia brought together the best qualities needed for a secretary-general," Basque Socialist chief Ramon Jauregui told reporters.
Having reached a consensus on Almunia, regional leaders took their recommendation to their separate delegations on Saturday night.

Delegates were also being given the chance to debate the merits of four other contenders -- ex-minister Jose Borrell, Extremadura regional president Juan Carlos Rodriguez Ibarra, Andalucia president Manuel Chaves and Castilla-La Mancha president Jose Bono.
Gonzalez, who had called for a "change of generations" in the party hierarchy, had promised not to interfere in the selection of his successor and gave no hint of his preference.

Nevertheless, Socialist leaders ended up picking one of Gonzalez' most stalwart loyalists. Almunia's membership in the Socialist Workers Party dates back to the mid-1970s when dictator Francisco Franco ruled Spain and Gonzalez was still in exile trying to steer the party away from Marxism.
As Gonzalez rose in stature, Almunia moved up through the party ranks, winning election as a parliamentary deputy from Madrid in 1979.
Gonzalez swept into power in 1982 on a surge of popular support to rebuld Spain after nearly 40 years of Franco rule.
Almunia served in Gonzalez' administration as labor minister from 1982 to 1986 and as minister of public administration from 1986 to 1991.

As the party's current parliamentary spokesman, Almunia has developed a high public profile. A recent opinion poll showed him with a public recognition rating of over 90 percent, among the best for Socialist politicians.

But the same poll, taken before Gonzalez' announcement on Friday, showed that only 1.7 percent of Socialist voters preferred him as a replacement for Gonzalez to lead the part into the next general election scheduled for the year 2000.

The selection of Gonzalez' successor was considered a wide-open race after the favorite of the party's rank-and-file, NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, immediately took himself out of the running.

A party official said Solana, a former Socialist foreign minister, wants to see NATO through the first stage of its planned eastward expansion but might be ready to return to Spanish politics after his term ends in 1999.
One day after Gonzalez' surprise announcement, the party faithful were still reeling from the impact.

But Socialist insiders mostly agreed that Gonzalez' departure was needed to begin a major overhaul of the party, which was left demoralized by its defeat by the centre-right Popular Party led by Jose Maria Aznar.

The Socialist-leaning daily El Pais praised Gonzalez for relinquishing power, saying it shows he is "a politican of the highest quality of his generation and that he understands it's time to give way to the next."
But the centre-right El Mundo newspaper suggested it was merely a "strategic withdrawal" that would allow him to keep control behind the scenes and eventually stage a comeback.
